A Scholar
from Jordan

Miss Mary George, M.B.E., Director E.A.W.,

IN The Electrical Age for January, 1963, Miss George described a visit she had paid to the pioneer vocational training centre for Arab girl refugees at Ramallah in Jordan. In her article Miss George mentioned that the Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust had been asked to consider the award of an exhibition to one of the Arab women staff at the centre to enable her to spend some months studying technical training methods in this country.

brief_extract:
A Scholar
from Jordan

Miss Mary George, M.B.E., Director E.A.W.,
with Miss Nada Sfeir in the E.A.W. Display Room

IN The Electrical Age for January, 1963, Miss George described a visit she had paid to the pioneer vocational training centre for Arab girl refugees at Ramallah in Jordan.

brief_context: Region where Dame Caroline Haslett supported women.
brief_extract: In her article Miss George mentioned that the Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust had been asked to consider the award of an exhibition to one of the Arab women staff at the centre to enable her to spend some months studying technical training methods in this country. This proposal commended itself to the Trust particularly in view of the interest Dame Caroline Haslett had taken in the role of women in the Middle East and also because nearly half of the cost of building and equipping the centre had been met by the United Kingdom World Refugee Fund. An exhibition was accordingly offered through the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) and the selected recipient is Miss Nada Sfeir who is the Domestic Bursar at the centre.

location_standardised: London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Where Miss Sfeir arrived for her course of study.
brief_extract: An exhibition was accordingly offered through the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) and the selected recipient is Miss Nada Sfeir who is the Domestic Bursar at the centre. Miss Sfeir arrived in London on January 10th of this year for a six months course of study and one of her first visits was to the E.A.W. Headquarters where she was welcomed by Miss George who interviewed her for The Electrical Age.

brief_context: Where Miss Sfeir was formerly a headmistress.
brief_extract: Headquarters where she was welcomed by Miss George who interviewed her for The Electrical Age. MISS GEORGE I understand, Miss Sfeir, that before joining the staff at Ramallah you were the headmistress of a girls' school in Bethlehem. How did you come to change your job?

location_standardised: London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Where Miss Sfeir will spend a term of study.
brief_extract: In the kitchen there is a head cook and her assistant with two helpers and there are 9 to wash up and prepare the vegetables. MISS GEORGE We have arranged for you to spend a term in the catering department of the Northern Polytechnic here in London, and after that to spend some little time outside London working with the warden of a university hostel, the superintendent of a hospital and a school meals organiser. Are there any particular problems which you would like to have help with?

brief_context: The location of the school where Miss Sfeir works.
brief_extract: At present they are working for much too long hours—usually about 14 hours a day—and I want to arrange their work in two shifts. I would like to see therefore how a place the same size as Ramallah is run in this country. MISS GEORGE I am sure this will be possible.

location_standardised: Aberdeen, Aberdeen City, Scotland, United Kingdom
brief_context: Site of the E.A.W. Annual Conference in May.
brief_extract: I think you will find that everyone here is most anxious to give you all the help they can and also to make you feel at home. The members of the E.A.W., particularly those who have contributed to the Trust, will be most keen to meet you and we hope that you will be our guest at our Annual Conference in Aberdeen from 1st to 3rd May. MISS SFEIR I do feel at home here already and everyone is most kind.

brief_context: Region Miss Sfeir wishes to visit to see lochs.
brief_extract: I never expected there would be so much concern for me when I came over here, a lone woman. I should like very much to go to Scotland and meet your members and to see the lochs about which I have heard so much. And is there not a monster somewhere?

brief_extract: And is there not a monster somewhere? MISS GEORGE Well, I can't promise that we shall be able to show you the Loch Ness Monster but we will certainly show you some of the beauties of Scotland. MISS SFEIR Thank you.

brief_context: Place where early window glass evidence was found.
brief_extract: Various translucent materials were used in early times for filling windows, including mica, horn, parchment, but none were as effective as glass. The fabrication of glass is depicted on Egyp-tian tombs of 1800 B.C., but there is no definite evidence of window glass in Italy until the 3rd century A.D. Churches had coloured glass win-dows in the 4th century, and by the end of the 12th century the art of staining glass had become popular in England, and small pieces of glass were leaded into mosaic-like patterns.

brief_context: Where stained glass and private windows became popular.
brief_extract: The fabrication of glass is depicted on Egyp-tian tombs of 1800 B.C., but there is no definite evidence of window glass in Italy until the 3rd century A.D. Churches had coloured glass win-dows in the 4th century, and by the end of the 12th century the art of staining glass had become popular in England, and small pieces of glass were leaded into mosaic-like patterns. Glass began to be used in windows of private houses in England as early as the 12th century, but it was not until the next century that glass was used extensively for domestic windows in this country.

brief_context: Mentioned in the context of Britain in Bloom year.
brief_extract: IN YOUR GARDEN by JOHN WARREN, N.D.H. THIS is Britain in Bloom year, and the British Holiday and Travel Association are organising competitions on a nation-wide basis in the hope that our towns and villages will be brightened up by extra floral displays during the summer, to make them more attractive to tourists. What a feast of gaiety and beauty we could have each summer, if all of us caught the spirit of this enterprise and made our gardens just that little bit more colourful this year!

brief_context: Origin of some newer geranium varieties mentioned.

brief_extract:
FINDING A HOME

MARY GEORGE, MBE, Director EAW,
describes an interesting housing project of the Over 40
Association for Women, of which she is Chairman

A corner of the electric kitchen

THIRTY years ago at the time of the econom-
ic depression the plight of many single
women was piteous, older women who lost
their jobs had little hopes of finding new ones,
and even women who were only 30 or 40 were
regarded as too old by employers. It was to help
such women in their difficulties that the Over
Thirty Association was founded in London. The
Association’s object was to provide cheap can-
teens, clubs that could offer warmth, rest and
company, and some retraining courses.

location_standardised: Chiswick, Hounslow, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Location of a house acquired for pension age applicants.
brief_extract:
The
Association decided therefore that its next ven-
ture in the housing field should be to provide a
home for a few of its pension age applicants. With
the aid of a large overdraft a suitable house was
acquired in the London Borough of Chiswick
and by last Christmas the six all-electric flatlets
into which it had been converted were ready for
occupation. Bearing in mind that the residents in this new
house would be at home far more than those with
full-time jobs living in our other houses, we
decided that we would be a little more extravagant
of space and provide kitchens separate from the
living rooms.

location_standardised: London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Area where most of the organisation's work is confined.
brief_extract: We were able to offer her a small room in one of our other houses where she remained until she moved into our Over Sixty House this year. We are a fairly small and modest organisation in the vast field of voluntary social service and most of our work is confined to the London area although we have recently been encouraged to extend our employment activities to Brighton where we have set up a combined service with another voluntary agency to help older women and pensioners (including men) who seek special assistance in finding employment. There is no doubt that if we were able to open an Over Forty house in Brighton there would be no shortage of deserving applicants but we certainly cannot afford to do this at the moment when we are struggling to pay for our Chiswick house.

brief_context: Refers to the UK's recognised colour code for electrical cables.
brief_extract:
Colour coding of flexibles
The colour coding of flexible cables of electrical equipment sometimes causes confusion. At the present time the recognised code in this country for the flexibles of domestic appliances is red for live, black for neutral, green for earth. This is not the case on the Continent, so that on some imported appliances, red for instance could be used for the earth, black for the live, and blue for the neutral according to its country of origin.

brief_context: Where plugs sold have clearly identified wiring pins.
brief_extract: In this country, the core colours which have been standardised for many years are red for the ‘live’ conductor, black for the ‘neutral’ and green for the ‘earth’ and if no electrical fittings or appliances were imported from any other country there would never be any doubt about which wire goes where! Plugs made and sold in Great Britain have their pins very clearly identified, either with a red sleeve or the letter ‘L’ for the live conductor, a black sleeve or the letter ‘N’ for the neutral and a green sleeve or the letter ‘E’ for the earth. And to simplify matters still further, the earth pin is always larger than either of the others.

brief_context: Refers to manufacturers using different colour codes for wiring.
brief_extract: So if you buy anything electrical of foreign origin which has a flex on it, make sure that it is colour-coded to the British standard before you fit a plug. If the cores are not labelled in any way don’t ever ‘take a chance’ because, just to quote one example, German manufacturers use the red core for the earth connection, instead of our green, which means that if you put the red wire on the live terminal of the plug, the metalwork of the appliance will become live and very dangerous. If there is any doubt at all about which lead goes where, take the thing to the nearest Approved Contractor on the National Inspection Council’s Roll (there are more than six thousand of them so you won’t have to go far!) and he will check it for you in a matter of minutes.

brief_context: The only country for which the Mint did not produce coins.
article_title: VISIT TO THE MINT AT BIRMINGHAM

brief_context: The country for which the Mint produced only tokens.
article_title: VISIT TO THE MINT AT BIRMINGHAM
brief_extract:
This factory is one of the most versatile members
had ever visited, in that if one section were short of
orders, there would be sufficient work in the others
to continue full employment, and although, at the
moment, the making of coins seems to be just a
subsidiary product they have in the past made coins
for every country in the world except the United
States, for whom they made tokens for their slot
machines. No coins have been made there for the
United Kingdom since 1919, but if the decimal system
were adopted, it is highly probable that they would
be given some of the work entailed in producing the
new coins. An interesting fact was that, although
our present-day so-called silver coins were made up
of 75% copper and 25% nickel, the original ones
made when the firm first commenced business had a
life expectancy of at least 100 years, and some are
believed to be still in existence.

brief_context: Location of a hut visited by the author.
brief_extract:
Lapps at Home
The hut at the Polar Circle was closed for the winter season, but a film was in the making and I was fortunate to see people in traditional Lapp costume with a herd of reindeer grazing peacefully in a nearby forest. In a small Lapp weaving works young girls were making the most exquisite rugs and mats in traditional local designs.

brief_context: Origin of a washing machine found in a Lapp farmhouse.
brief_extract: (A Lapp's wealth is recognised by the head of reindeer and one does not ask how many he has!) It was interesting to observe in this traditional home the way in which electricity had blended so wonderfully with antiquity—electric lighting yet candles on the table; a large oven heated by wood from the local forest, yet a modern electric cooker in full use. Here in this remote farmhouse was an electric iron, a British washing machine and spin dryer, vacuum cleaner, and water supply operated by electric pump. There were 10 people including two paid hands to help on the land which consisted of 18 hectares of arable land for hay, wheat and rye, and a further 232 hectares of forestry, in all 250 hectares (about 620 acres).

location_standardised: Seaton Delaval, Northumberland, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: The hall built for the de la Val family.
brief_extract: It served as the private chapel of the Norman Castle or Tower and succeeding houses of the de la Val family which stood nearby. It continued to serve as the private chapel of the de la Val family until the building of the present Seaton Delaval Hall in 1718-28, and was the burial place of the family until 1771. On the death of the last male de la Val in 1814, the Hall and estate came into the possession, through the female line, of the family of Astley of Melton Constable, Norfolk, and the church was the private chapel of that family until 1891, when they gave it to be the parish church of the newly formed parish of Delaval.

location_standardised: Melton Constable, Norfolk, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: The ancestral home of the Astley family.
brief_extract:
It continued to serve as the private chapel of the de la Val family until the building of the present Seaton Delaval Hall in 1718-28, and was the burial place of the family until 1771. On the death of the last male de la Val in 1814, the Hall and estate came into the possession, through the female line, of the family of Astley of Melton Constable, Norfolk, and the church was the private chapel of that family until 1891, when they gave it to be the parish church of the newly formed parish of Delaval. Outstanding features

The chief glory of the church lies in its two perfect Norman arches with zig-zag ornamentation, a style of architecture introduced at the time of the Conquest.

brief_context: Whose arms appear on the 'Prince of Wales Window'.
brief_extract: In the south wall of the choir the 'Prince of Wales Window', bought in 1841 by Sir Jacob Astley, First Lord Hastings, after the revival of the title, represents a medieval figure, perhaps Edward, the Black Prince, kneeling before an open Bible. On his coat of mail are the arms of France and of England. The bell turret has what is believed to be a pre-reformation bell.

brief_context: Location where Lord Delaval cut a harbour entrance.
brief_extract: The bell turret has what is believed to be a pre-reformation bell. Hatchments (or achievements) commemorating the de la Val and Astley families are a feature of the church, and include Edward John Hussey de la Val, designer of the lightning conductor, and the last male de la Val (died 1814); Sir Francis Blake de la Val, the only de la Val who was a Knight of the Bath (died 1771); John Hussey de la Val, the only Lord Delaval, who cut the entrance to the harbour at Seaton Sluice; Sir Jacob Astley, who revived the title Baron Hastings (died 1859); Jacob Henry Astley, Baron Hastings, who put a roof on the central part of the Hall to preserve it from further destruction (died 1871); and the Rev. de la Val Loftus Astley, Baron Hastings (died 1872).

brief_context: Environment from which many house plants originate.
brief_extract:
In fact such plants will be quite happy in a north window, where they will receive good even light throughout the day, but they must be moved back from the window to a warmer position on cold nights. Atmospheric moisture
This is also very important to house plants, many of which hail from tropical forests where the atmosphere is highly humid at all times, and the atmosphere in the average living room is much too dry for them. An easy and fairly effective way of providing this moisture, is to place the plants in an outer container, and pack the space between the pot and the sides of the container with moist peat.

brief_context: Regions where some plants thrive in cooler conditions.
brief_extract: As soon as these symptoms are noted, take steps to improve the light, or move the plant nearer to the window. The temperature will obviously depend on the type of plant being grown, those of tropical origin will need higher temperatures while those from temperate regions will thrive where it is cooler. Cyclamen do not require high temperatures, and will be quite happy in a room where the temperature does not fall below 45-50 deg.

brief_context: Region where the generator is the largest in operation
article_title: VISIT TO THORPE MARSH POWER STATION
brief_extract:
On the last day of 1963 the first of the two 550,000 kw
turbo-alternators to be installed at Thorpe Marsh made
its first official contribution to the national demand for
power, when it was synchronised with the national grid
and supergrid systems. It is the largest generator to come
into commercial operation in Western Europe, and will
play a large part in helping to meet the ever increasing
national demands made on the power stations. Although Thorpe Marsh will not be in full operation
until possibly early in 1965, the Wetherby members got
a wonderful picture of a giant new Yorkshire Power
station using another Yorkshire fuel—coal.

brief_context: Location of the 'twin' nuclear station opened in 1963.
article_title: VISIT TO BERKELEY NUCLEAR POWER STATION
brief_extract:
Work at Berkeley was started in 1957 and the station 
began feeding into the National Grid in June 1962. The 
official opening by HRH the Duke of Edinburgh was 
performed jointly with the 'twin' station at Bradwell in 
Essex in April 1963. With an installed capacity of 322 mw and an output of
275 mw Berkeley is the smallest of nine nuclear stations in 
the present CEGB programme.

brief_extract:
They were pleased to find

brief_context: Country from which ships and cars originated.
article_title: VISIT TO FELIXSTOWE DOCK AND RAILWAY COMPANY
brief_extract:
There were British cars for export, and German 
cars were being imported. One ship was taking on explo- 
sives, and all the time there were cranes like giant giraffes 
going up and down, trains shunting, lorries reversing,
people dashing here, there and everywhere, but it was a 
very organised commotion, and in between it all sat the 
ships from Germany, Norway, Denmark, Sweden and 
Holland, seemingly undisturbed. Then there were the tank farms, containing petroleum, 
fuel oils, hydrocarbon, industrial solvents and some, 
separated by bund walls and water-filled ditches, con- 
taining toxic bulk liquids, which because of their extremely 
low flash point have to be handled very cautiously and 
are loaded by flameproof electric pumps operated by 
remote control.

location_standardised: Rotherham, South Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Town associated with the author Mrs. B. Elders.
brief_extract:
B. Elders, Magazine Secretary, Rotherham

Members visited Cadbury's chocolate factory where 
press-button control is the servant of the craftsman. In- 
gredients are pumped to the giant storage tanks, and are 
quickly and accurately measured by electronic computers 
and fed to the mixers making hundreds of biscuits; the 
mixture is then put on another machine for chocolate 
covering.

where members had a good 'look round', and again noted 
the extensive contribution of electricity. 12
